content: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to an infection that affects the female reproductive organs, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. As the infection progresses, it can lead to the formation of scar tissue and adhesions that involve nearby tissues and organs. In severe cases, this can result in tissue necrosis, with or without the formation of abscesses. Pus may also be released into the peritoneal cavity. Notably, two-thirds of patients with laparoscopic evidence of prior PID were unaware they had ever experienced the condition. PID is frequently associated with sexually transmitted infections (STIs), as it is a common consequence of such infections. While the term PID is often used to describe bacterial infections, it can also encompass viral, fungal, or parasitic infections. The classification of PID should consider the specific organs involved, the stage of the infection, and the causative organism(s). Although STIs are a common cause, other routes of infection include lymphatic spread, postpartum or post-abortion complications, intrauterine device (IUD)-related infections, and hematogenous spread. PID occurs when bacteria ascend from the vagina or cervix into the upper reproductive organs. While various organisms can cause PID, the majority of cases are linked to Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, two prevalent bacterial STIs. Certain factors increase the risk of developing PID. These include a history of PID, recent sexual activity, the onset of menstruation, the presence of an IUD, or having a partner with an STI. Acute PID is unlikely in the absence of recent sexual activity or IUD use. Although PID can be treated and cured, the damage caused by the infection may be irreversible. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications, such as damage to the reproductive system. Since early gonococcal infections may be asymptomatic, regular screening is essential for high-risk individuals, such as those with multiple sexual partners, a history of unprotected sex, or symptoms suggestive of an STI. Screening is also recommended for patients who have undergone pelvic procedures, including postpartum care, miscarriage, or abortion. If the infection is confined to the lower reproductive tract, timely treatment can prevent complications. However, infections involving the fallopian tubes or ovaries are more likely to result in serious outcomes. Diagnosing PID can be challenging due to its often subtle and nonspecific symptoms. Many cases go undetected because patients or healthcare providers fail to recognize the significance of mild symptoms. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical findings, as there are no definitive tests for PID. Some patients may be asymptomatic, while others may present with fever, cervical motion tenderness, lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, painful intercourse, or irregular menstrual bleeding. Additional symptoms may include foul-smelling vaginal discharge, painful urination, or, in rare cases, pain in the right upper abdomen. It is important to note that PID can cause significant harm even in the absence of noticeable symptoms. Laboratory tests are used to identify signs of infection, but no single test is sufficiently sensitive or specific to diagnose PID. Common laboratory findings include elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and white blood cell (WBC) count. A sensitive serum pregnancy test is essential to rule out ectopic pregnancy. Gram staining and smears may help identify rare or severe pathogens. Pelvic ultrasound is a valuable diagnostic tool for PID. It can detect abnormalities such as enlarged fallopian tubes or the presence of abscesses. Ultrasound is also useful in differentiating PID from other conditions, such as ectopic pregnancy, particularly after six weeks of gestation. Additional diagnostic procedures, such as culdocentesis, can help distinguish between hemoperitoneum (caused by conditions like ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemorrhagic cyst) and pelvic sepsis (caused by conditions like salpingitis, ruptured pelvic abscess, or ruptured appendix). Treatment for PID typically involves antibiotic therapy, which is tailored to the causative organism. If symptoms do not improve within two to three days of starting antibiotics, the patient should return to the hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Antibiotics may be administered orally or intravenously, depending on the severity of the infection. Hospitalization may be necessary in cases of tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness, immunodeficiency, pregnancy, cervical incompetence, or other potentially life-threatening conditions. Treating sexual partners is a critical component of managing PID to prevent reinfection. Partners of patients diagnosed with PID within the past six months should also receive treatment. Psychotherapy is often recommended for women diagnosed with PID, as they may experience anxiety about the possibility of recurrence. Open communication with a healthcare provider, particularly a gynecologist, is essential for addressing concerns and ensuring appropriate follow-up care. In cases where symptoms persist or an abscess does not resolve, surgical intervention may be required. Complications of PID, such as chronic pelvic pain and scarring, can be challenging to manage, although some patients may experience improvement following surgery.
